method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409) 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era' (2025), 15 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC 4.0 (read at NCBI efetch JATS XML <license> element for PMC12706554 (Europe PMC fullTextXML returned no body)). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522) 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study' (published 31 January 2024), 12 claims; LICENCE: © 2024 Zhang et al.; published and licensed by Dove Medical Press under CC BY-NC 3.0 (unported) and the Dove terms (https://www.dovepress.com/terms.php) (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC10838494). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, a single-centre retrospective study of 127 inpatients with refractory auricular perichondritis in eastern China (Zhang et al. 2024, CC BY-NC 3.0), for causes, culture yield, fungal infection and antibiotic susceptibility. S1's claims and anchors are unchanged. Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S2 Table 2 (isolates by cause). S1 Tables 1–4 and S2 Tables 1, 3 and 4 have merged cells or ragged rows and were not extracted.

claims.claim: **Auricular perichondritis is inflammation of the perichondrium of the ear, most often an infection, usually with *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*.** Organisms get in through small breaks in the skin (injury, insect bites, self-injury) or bigger insults such as piercing or burns.
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Untreated, it can deform the ear permanently ('cauliflower ear') and spread to deeper tissues,** so diagnosis and treatment should be prompt.
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cartilage ('high') piercing is a common trigger.** Infection afterwards is not rare, because most piercers are not health professionals and may not know or follow antiseptic practice.
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Two patterns.** Piercing-related cases were much younger (mean age 25 against 51 years). Cases without a piercing followed herpes zoster, recent ear surgery such as tympanoplasty, allergic skin reactions, trauma or other skin breaks.
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cases without a piercing more often had comorbidities (diabetes, smoking, immunosuppression), involved the ear diffusely, and caused fever or enlarged nodes.** Piercing cases were more local and formed an abscess more often (28.3% against 13.4%).
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diabetes may delay presentation,** perhaps because of reduced sensation. The authors suggest this delay, together with comorbidity, explains why cases without a piercing are more often complicated.
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Why it damages the ear:** the cartilage has no blood vessels of its own and is fed by the perichondrium, so infection there can starve it, leading to necrosis and liquefaction. The disease moves fast, and poor management risks deep soft-tissue or systemic infection.
claims.locator: Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522), 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study', published 31 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10838494/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **In a hospital cohort the leading cause was ear surgery, not piercing:** 37.8% followed aural surgery (29.1% tympanoplasty) and 18.1% trauma, of which only six were piercings and five frostbite. No cause was found in 37.0%.
claims.locator: Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522), 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study', published 31 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10838494/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Of cultured cases, *P. aeruginosa* and *Staphylococcus aureus* were the main organisms.** *P. aeruginosa* was more frequent after piercing (52.4% against 20.6%). Other organisms, including *Enterobacter*, *Morganella*, *Aspergillus* and *Actinomyces*, were much more frequent without a piercing.
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Culture before starting systemic antibiotics in every new case, piercing-related or not.** Two reasons: cases without a piercing often involve organisms other than Pseudomonas, and fluoroquinolone resistance is rising.
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **An abscess is the strongest warning sign.** It was the only independent predictor of complications (odds ratio 35.75 across the whole cohort). Complications affected 29.5% of patients overall.
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cultures are often negative once antibiotics have started:** swabs were taken in 73.2% and only 59.1% grew anything, which the authors put down to prior outpatient antibiotics and the little discharge these ears produce.
claims.locator: Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522), 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study', published 31 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10838494/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Ask the laboratory for fungal culture, especially after ear surgery.** Fungi made up 23.0% of isolates (*Aspergillus* 18.0%); fungal infection was found in 41.7% of post-surgical cases against 7.1% after trauma, and went with immune-related comorbidity and longer admissions.
claims.locator: Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522), 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study', published 31 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10838494/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ***P. aeruginosa* was the commonest isolate (49.2%), and in piercing-related cases it was the organism every time (100%).** Other series report from 20.4% (Denmark) to 60.6% (India).
claims.locator: Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522), 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study', published 31 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10838494/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Isolates by cause in S2 (61 in all):** gram-negative bacteria 55.7%, nearly all *P. aeruginosa*; gram-positive 21.3% (coagulase-negative staphylococci 8.2%, *S. aureus* 4.9%, viridans streptococci and *S. pyogenes* 3.3% each); fungi 23.0% (*Aspergillus* 18.0%, *Candida* 4.9%). After surgery (24 isolates): *P. aeruginosa* 45.8%, *Aspergillus* 29.2% and *Candida* 12.5%. After trauma (14 isolates): *P. aeruginosa* 64.3% and coagulase-negative staphylococci 21.4%.
claims.locator: Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522), 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study', published 31 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10838494/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Gram-negative isolates were almost all susceptible to amikacin (100%), cefepime (93.9%), meropenem (97.1%) and ceftazidime (90.9%),** but only 67.4% to levofloxacin and 65.2% to ciprofloxacin.
claims.locator: Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522), 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study', published 31 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10838494/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Gram-positive isolates were all susceptible to vancomycin (100%),** but few to penicillin G (30.8%), ceftriaxone (20.0%), levofloxacin (41.7%), ciprofloxacin (30.8%) or erythromycin (15.4%).
claims.locator: Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522), 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study', published 31 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10838494/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Be cautious with a fluoroquinolone as the first empirical choice.** Pseudomonas susceptibility to fluoroquinolones fell over the decade, and multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas appeared (22.2% of Pseudomonas cases in 2018–2022, none in 2013–2017), all resistant to gentamicin, ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin.
claims.locator: Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522), 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study', published 31 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10838494/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Gram-positive organisms fell from 34.6% to 11.4% of isolates between 2013–2017 and 2018–2022,** while gram-negative and fungal isolates rose; the authors link this to wide outpatient use of amoxicillin-clavulanate and first- and second-generation cephalosporins.
claims.locator: Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522), 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study', published 31 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10838494/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Usual empirical treatment is ciprofloxacin, with incision and drainage of any abscess under the perichondrium;** necrotic cartilage often has to be debrided carefully as well.
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Abscess: incise and drain and give intravenous antibiotics from the start,** whether or not there is fever or lymphadenopathy.
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Give antibiotics intravenously as well when the patient has diabetes, is immunosuppressed or smokes heavily.**
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **With no comorbidity, no abscess and no systemic features,** the authors consider topical treatment, alone or with an oral antibiotic, a safe way to start.
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In hospital, start empirical cover against *Pseudomonas*.** In S2, 78.7% got an anti-pseudomonal first regimen, most often ceftazidime alone (47.2%); the best option for people allergic to cephalosporins is still unknown.
claims.locator: Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522), 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study', published 31 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10838494/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Expect a real chance of treatment failure:** 18.3% needed at least one change of regimen for poor response and 29.5% needed further drainage in hospital. Mean hospital stay was 5.3 days and mean total treatment 11.1 days.
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Recent ear surgery was associated with a complicated course,** and patients with complications had been admitted later than those without (a mean of 12.2 against 4.7 days).
claims.locator: Ungar OJ, Bursztyn N, Shilo S, et al., The Laryngoscope 135(12):4693-4702 (doi 10.1002/lary.32409), 'Auricular Perichondritis in the Cartilage Piercing Era', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12706554/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refractory disease responds slowly:** in S2 only 62.2% had fully settled by discharge, and six of the 71 followed up had a recurrence within 30 days.
claims.locator: Zhang, Zhang, Pu, et al., Infection and Drug Resistance 17:377-386 (doi 10.2147/IDR.S434522), 'Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study', published 31 January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10838494/, retrieved 2026-09-24
